analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to get your signed permission before sharing your financial information with outside companies.
analysis.headline: A House bill to give customers veto power over the sharing of their financial records was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in February 2011 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law in effect since 1999, banks and other financial companies can sell or share your personal financial information with outside companies unless you actively tell them to stop — and most customers never see or respond to those notices. This bill would flip that: a bank could not hand your nonpublic financial information to an unaffiliated company unless you signed a separate, plain-language consent form. It would also bar banks from punishing customers who refuse to consent, tighten what banks may share with their own affiliates, ban selling your account numbers for marketing, and require a one-page, easy-to-read model notice.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank and credit card customers, who would gain real control over who sees their account activity, balances, and purchase records. People who currently discard the dense opt-out notices that arrive with statements would get a single signed form instead, and a bank could not deny them a product or offer worse terms for saying no.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the current opt-out system — where your information is shared unless you object — with an opt-in system requiring your signed consent on a separate form before any disclosure to an unaffiliated third party [S2][S3].
Prohibits a bank from discriminating against you, denying you a product, or offering worse terms because you declined to consent [S2][S3].
Restricts what banks may share with their own affiliates unless the customer has been notified and has not objected, and limits reuse of that information beyond the affiliate [S3].
Bans disclosing credit card, debit card, and deposit account numbers to outside companies for telemarketing, direct mail, or email marketing [S3].
Directs federal regulators to create a one-page model consent form written in short, plain sentences with large type, replacing the dense privacy notices consumers currently receive [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit card issuers, and other financial firms would bear the compliance cost of new consent forms and would lose revenue from selling or sharing customer data with marketers. Customers might see fewer bundled offers and discounts that are funded by data sharing, since the bill allows incentives for consenting but cuts off sharing without it.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows banks to offer incentives or discounts in exchange for consent, so customers who want the best deal could still end up signing away their data [S3].

It keeps broad exceptions: banks may still share with affiliates after opt-out, share under joint-offering and affinity-partner arrangements, and disclose data for servicing, fraud prevention, and other listed purposes — so a large share of data flows would continue [S3].
Banks would face new compliance costs designing consent forms and tracking consumer directions, costs that could be passed to customers through fees [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — moving from opt-out to signed opt-in before your financial data goes to outside companies — directly addresses a real, long-standing gap in consumer privacy, and the discrimination ban keeps saying no from becoming costly. The main honest costs are compliance burden on banks and fewer data-funded discount offers, and the bill's own carve-outs mean it would not stop all sharing. On balance it is a straightforward consumer protection with modest, acknowledged costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2011, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and sent to a subcommittee a month later — and then went nowhere; the Congress ended in January 2013 without the bill ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jackie Speier introduced the bill on February 11, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S1][S5].
On March 23, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, was never reported out of committee, and was never considered on the House floor [S5].
Eight House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, credit card issuers, and data marketers are better off: the existing opt-out system stayed in place, so financial companies can keep sharing and selling customer information with outside firms, and consumers never got a choice in the matter.

industries.note: The bill would replace the current opt-out system with a signed opt-in before sharing customer data with outside companies, cutting off a revenue stream from selling customer information and adding compliance costs. It also bars banks from retaliating against customers who refuse, so the industry's interest here runs against customers' control over their own data [S2][S3].

These companies buy or receive consumer financial data from banks to fuel telemarketing, direct mail, and email campaigns. The opt-in requirement and the ban on sharing account numbers for marketing would sharply cut off their supply of data [S3].

industries.industry: Affinity partners and retail card issuers
industries.note: The bill keeps some sharing with affinity partners under contract and confidentiality requirements, but bans the practice for retail-branded credit cards and limits the data disclosed to names and contact details [S3].
The ban on sharing account numbers for marketing specifically excludes consumer reporting agencies, so the flow of information to credit bureaus would continue as before [S3].
